prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
Two people, whom I will call Asha and Ben, want to agree on a secret number. They have never met and share no password. The only way they can talk is a line that anyone can listen to, and a third person, Eve, hears every word they say. Asha and Ben want to finish with a number that both of them know and Eve does not, so that they can use it as the key for scrambling their later messages. For most of history this was thought to be impossible, since a key had to be agreed beforehand, usually by meeting or by sending a courier. In 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a method that needs neither. Their method rests on a kind of sum that is easy to do forwards and very slow to undo.

The first thing to know is clock arithmetic. On a twelve-hour clock, five hours after nine o'clock is two o'clock, because the count starts again at one after twelve. The number you finish on is the remainder left when you divide by twelve. Nothing requires the clock to have twelve hours, and in this explanation we will use one with 23. Any number we calculate is replaced by its remainder after dividing by 23, so 30 becomes 7 and 50 becomes 4. Mathematicians call the size of the clock the modulus.

The second thing is powers. Five to the power of three means 5 times 5 times 5, which is 125. On the 23-hour clock, 125 becomes 10, since 23 goes into 125 five times with 10 left over. If we write down 5 to the power of 1, 2, 3 and so on, always reducing by 23, the results are 5, 2, 10, 4, 20, 8 and then 17, 16, 11, 9. The numbers jump about with no pattern that you can see. Working forwards is easy. You pick a power, multiply, and read off the answer. Working backwards is the hard direction. If someone tells you that some power of 5 came out as 8 on this clock and asks which power it was, the only general method is to try them one by one until 8 turns up. Here it turns up at the sixth, so the problem is trivial, but the principle is what matters.

Now the exchange itself. Asha and Ben first agree, out loud and in front of Eve, on two public numbers, which are the clock size 23 and the base 5. These are not secret. Then each of them chooses a number of their own and keeps it to themselves. Asha chooses 6 and Ben chooses 15. Asha works out 5 to the power of 6 on the clock, which is 8, and sends 8 to Ben. Ben works out 5 to the power of 15, which is 19, and sends 19 to Asha. Eve hears 23, 5, 8 and 19. She does not hear 6 or 15, because those never leave Asha and Ben.

Next each of them takes the number they received and raises it to their own private power. Asha takes Ben's 19 and raises it to the power of 6, which gives 2 on the clock. Ben takes Asha's 8 and raises it to the power of 15, which also gives 2. They have arrived at the same number, and it was never sent down the line. The reason it matches is that Asha's calculation amounts to 5 raised to the power of 15 and then to the power of 6, and Ben's amounts to 5 raised to the power of 6 and then to the power of 15. In both cases the total power is 6 times 15, or 90, and the order of multiplying does not change the product. The shared secret is therefore 5 to the power of 90 on the clock, and that is 2.

Eve's position is as follows. She knows the clock, the base, and the two numbers that were sent. To find the secret she needs either 6 or 15. She can look for them by trying powers of 5 until she meets 8 or 19, and with a clock of 23 that takes a minute with a pencil. Real systems use a far larger clock. A typical modulus today is a prime number of 2,048 binary digits, which is about 617 decimal digits long, and the private numbers are of similar size. The count of possible private numbers is much greater than the roughly 10 to the power of 80 atoms thought to be in the observable universe. No method is known that lets an ordinary computer find the private number from the public ones in a practical time. Asha and Ben can still do their own part quickly, because there are short ways to compute a huge power, such as squaring the number over and over and multiplying together only the squares that are needed.

This is where the name public-key comes from. Each person ends up holding a private number and a public one. Asha's private number is 6 and her public number is 8. Ben's are 15 and 19. Anyone may see the public numbers. Combining one person's public number with the other's private number gives the shared secret, while the two public numbers alone do not. The idea was announced in 1976, though the British signals agency GCHQ had reached similar results a few years earlier, through the work of James Ellis, Clifford Cocks and Malcolm Williamson, and kept them secret until 1997. A second public-key scheme, published in 1977 by Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman, uses a different hard problem, which is splitting a very large number into its prime factors. It lets a person encrypt a message directly with someone's public number so that only the holder of the matching private number can read it.

The secret that comes out of the exchange is not used on the messages themselves. In the example it is 2, which is of no use, but in practice it is a number hundreds of digits long, or a 256-bit number if a variant based on elliptic curves is used. Either is passed to a fast ordinary cipher such as AES, which scrambles the actual data. Public-key sums are slow compared with that cipher, so they are used for the opening step only. When your browser connects to a website with a padlock beside the address, an exchange of this kind takes place in a fraction of a second, with fresh private numbers each time. Because the private numbers are thrown away afterwards, someone who recorded the conversation and later steals the website's long-term keys still cannot read it.

There are two limits worth knowing. The first is that the exchange does not tell you who you are talking to. If Eve can do more than listen, she can sit in the middle, pretend to be Ben when speaking to Asha and pretend to be Asha when speaking to Ben, and finish with one secret shared with each of them. Websites deal with this by holding a certificate, which is a statement that a given public number belongs to a given site, signed using another public-key scheme by an organisation that browsers already trust. My view is that most real failures of this system have come from the checking of identity and from mistakes in software, and not from weakness in the sums. The second limit is that a large quantum computer running an algorithm published by Peter Shor in 1994 could undo the hard problem in the exchange described here. A machine of the needed size does not exist yet, and standards bodies have already published replacement methods, which some browsers now use alongside the older one.
